on_watch_sysfs_reading_traps.rule: Reading sysfs on a watch is not uniformly safe or uniform. Time out EVERY read individually in a probe script, and resolve multi-value sources BY NAME.
on_watch_sysfs_reading_traps.blocking_node: `/sys/power/wakeup_count` BLOCKS on read — documented kernel behaviour, it waits until wakeup events can be captured. It hung an entire capability probe on nemo: the script returned NO output at all, not even the fields already gathered, which read as an adb fault. Never read it from a sampler.
on_watch_sysfs_reading_traps.no_backlight_class: These watches have NO `/sys/class/backlight`. The panel is exposed under the LED class as `/sys/class/leds/lcd-backlight/brightness`. Confirmed absent on nemo, empty on catfish (2026-07-31). Code written against the usual Linux path silently records an empty screen-state column forever.
on_watch_sysfs_reading_traps.battery_nodes_can_disagree: catfish reports capacity=50 on `/sys/class/power_supply/battery` and capacity=100 on `nanohub_fuelgauge-0` AT THE SAME INSTANT. Read the gauge by NAME with a fixed preference order (nanohub_fuelgauge-* first), and RECORD which node was read alongside the value, so a trace can be re-read later if the preference turns out wrong. moWerk's read (a hypothesis, not settled): the non-50 value has always been the correct one, and catfish's MCU for the secondary LCD is likely the good source.
on_watch_sysfs_reading_traps.no_current_sensor_at_all: nemo reports `current_now = 0` forever. A tidy log full of zeros means NO INSTRUMENT, not no drain — it must be named as such, or the slow capacity-delta method silently gets skipped.

watch_rtc_is_not_a_timing_source.rule: Never compute elapsed time on a watch from its wall clock. Use `/proc/uptime`, which no clock adjustment can move.
watch_rtc_is_not_a_timing_source.evidence: Measured against the host at the same instant, 2026-07-31: catfish's clock was 130 DAYS behind (watch said 2026-03-23); nemo's was ~2 HOURS ahead. Both were recording perfectly well — this is the normal state of a device that has not synced, not a broken watch.
watch_rtc_is_not_a_timing_source.the_subtle_part: A CONSTANT offset is harmless to deltas — epoch-based and uptime-based timing agree exactly on a steadily-wrong clock. So a test built on a large steady skew PASSES against an implementation using the wrong clock. The discriminating cases are a clock STEPPED mid-trace (invents elapsed time) and a clock FROZEN across suspend (hides it).
watch_rtc_is_not_a_timing_source.cross_check: Within one boot, epoch delta and uptime delta should match. A divergence IS a clock adjustment, and is invisible if you only look at one of the two.
watch_rtc_is_not_a_timing_source.bonus: A DROP in uptime between two samples is a REBOOT, so reboot detection falls out of any uptime-stamped log for free. Never compute elapsed time across that break.
watch_rtc_is_not_a_timing_source.report_dont_correct: Measure skew against the host and REPORT it. A silently corrected timestamp looks trustworthy; an obviously wrong one does not.

never_wake_the_watch_recording_pattern.rule: An on-watch recorder must add ZERO wakeups. On a watch the expensive part of a periodic job is the wakeup, not the reading — a probe that wakes the CPU to record the battery is draining the battery it measures.
never_wake_the_watch_recording_pattern.primitive: A systemd timer with `WakeSystem=false` (the default; state it explicitly, it is the whole design) firing a `Type=oneshot` service that appends one line and exits. Such a timer arms no RTC alarm — it fires only when the system is already awake, or on the next wake after the interval. Set `AccuracySec` deliberately LARGE (minutes) so systemd coalesces the firing with wakeups that were happening anyway. Nothing resident between samples: no loop, no wakelock, nothing to leak.
never_wake_the_watch_recording_pattern.gaps_are_data: The resulting samples are irregular and full of holes, which is the second half of the design. A gap means the watch genuinely slept through it — the standby behaviour you want to measure, and exactly what a regular sampler destroys by waking through it.
never_wake_the_watch_recording_pattern.prior_art_attribution: dodoradio got here first. asteroid-sensorlogd's README (2023) states the same principle almost verbatim: 'Sensorlogd will only record data when the CPU is already running. It does not schedule any wakeups... This is intended as a crude form of wear detection and as a power-saving measure.' The WEAR-DETECTION framing is the better one — if the watch wakes, someone is wearing it. Do NOT present this architecture as novel.
never_wake_the_watch_recording_pattern.trigger_choice_matters: sensorlogd triggers on MCE `display_status_ind` (display turns ON). That is an excellent proxy for 'a human is present' — and the WRONG trigger for POWER telemetry, because screen-on IS the expensive state and standby drain happens in the dark. A systemd timer fires on ANY wake, which is what power measurement needs.
never_wake_the_watch_recording_pattern.measured: catfish, 2026-07-31: 3 samples across 50 minutes undocked, one unbroken 49-minute gap, asleep_fraction 0.978. A 5-minute sampler would have produced ~10 samples there by waking the watch ten times.
never_wake_the_watch_recording_pattern.the_precondition_that_gates_everything: A probe must prove its OWN battery cost is in the noise before any number it produces is quotable — A/B on one watch, probe installed vs not, refereed by a real drain test. A null result (both arms inside the noise) is NOT a pass: it means the measurement lacked the sensitivity to detect the cost.

usb_ssh_developer_mode_first_boot_no_dhc.rule: A watch that cold-boots into developer_mode (USB-SSH) does NOT answer DHCP on its FIRST enumeration. One USB power cycle and it leases within seconds. Any host tooling that reaches watches over USB-SSH must cycle the port before concluding the watch is unreachable.
usb_ssh_developer_mode_first_boot_no_dhc.host_side_evidence: NetworkManager retries every 45s and logs `dhcp4 (<iface>): state changed no lease` indefinitely; the interface carries only a link-local IPv6 address. Reproduced 2026-08-01 on two AsteroidOS watches (dory, sturgeon) on the w541 rig.
usb_ssh_developer_mode_first_boot_no_dhc.why_it_cascades: No IPv4 on the host link means no route to 192.168.2.0/24, so the shared default 192.168.2.15 is unreachable and no SSH transport can be built. A tool then reports the watch as unreachable, which is CORRECT but looks like a tooling bug.
ruled_out_with_evidence: cradle / link churn — a watch with ZERO re-enumerations over 3+ minutes still got no lease
several RNDIS links colliding — reproduced with the failing watch as the ONLY link on the bus
host NetworkManager config — the working and failing connection profiles were identical (ipv4.method:auto, autoconnect:yes)
per-watch IP allocation stealing the route — a stray brings its own route as soon as it leases (192.168.2.1/24 arrived <10s after a cycle)
usb_ssh_developer_mode_first_boot_no_dhc.note: The reason the watch does not answer until re-plugged is device-side and was not diagnosed here. Historically USB-SSH on the fixed 192.168.2.15 was the standard path and worked, so this is a transition-into-developer_mode issue rather than a property of developer_mode itself.
usb_ssh_developer_mode_first_boot_no_dhc.fix_pattern: Mirror the adb-side recovery that already exists in asteroid-docking-bay: `not enumerating -> power-cycling once`. A stray that stays unreachable for a couple of probe retries should get exactly one power cycle, then self-heal.

podman_image_build_invocation.rule: AsteroidOS images are built in a podman container (NOT docker) from ~/Git/asteroid. The w541 builds NATIVE bare metal instead. Recorded 2026-08-01 because it was missing and had to be re-derived mid-task.

podman_image_build_invocation.then: inside the same container pattern: `. ./prepare-build.sh <machine>` then `bitbake asteroid-image`. Several hours from a cold cache.
podman_image_build_invocation.MOUNT_PATHS_DIFFER_PER_MACHINE: Do NOT copy the mount paths from another host — they are not the same on e15 and p14s. Check the actual mounts on the machine you are on before building. On p14s (verified 2026-08-01) they are /mnt/auto/w541sstate and /mnt/auto/w541downloads. Note /mnt/w541sstate and /mnt/w541downloads also exist there as EMPTY stubs and are NOT the right paths.

cpu_limits.e15: limit to 10 — its desktop still crashes above 12 threads under full load

podman_image_build_invocation.sstate_and_downloads_come_from_the_w541: Both are sshfs systemd automounts pointing at mo@mo-w541-eos:/mnt/storage/AsteroidOS/build/{sstate-cache,downloads} — sstate read-only, downloads read-write. The build machines share the w541's cache.
podman_image_build_invocation.THE_SILENT_FAILURE: If the automount units are not ACTIVE, the mount points are EMPTY DIRECTORIES rather than an error. The build then runs with no sstate mirror and no download cache — a cache-warm build silently becomes a cold multi-hour one, with nothing in the output saying so. ALWAYS verify the mounts are populated before starting: `ls /mnt/auto/w541sstate | wc -l` must be non-zero.
podman_image_build_invocation.after_a_reboot: The units are `enabled` but were found `inactive dead` after a p14s reboot (2026-08-01) — likely network-online ordering against wifi. Start them with `sudo systemctl start mnt-auto-w541sstate.automount mnt-auto-w541downloads.automount`. This needs interactive sudo (fingerprint), so an agent must ask moWerk to run it.
podman_image_build_invocation.asteroid_repo_is_not_a_git_workspace: ~/Git/asteroid is OFF LIMITS for git operations. Source updates are managed solely by prepare-build.sh. Work happens in task-transient workspaces that are cleaned up afterwards, leaving a clean upstream build state — check for and clean another session's leftovers before starting.
podman_image_build_invocation.machine_ownership: These hosts are shared between several agent sessions. The w541 is usually owned by the a-d-b agent (it drives the watch rig and builds test images). Confirm ownership with moWerk before taking a build machine.
podman_image_build_invocation.status: FINAL STATE as of 2026-08-01, after weeks of consolidating and fixing the build servers. Only remaining work is hardening the e15.

three_machine_architecture.w541: THE cache owner. Builds NATIVE bare metal, no container. Holds the one canonical sstate-cache + downloads on its dedicated SSD at /mnt/storage/AsteroidOS/build/{sstate-cache,downloads} (23 GB sstate as of 2026-08-01). Also runs the watch rig and asteroid-docking-bay.
three_machine_architecture.p14s: podman + the asteroidos-toolchain image. --cpus=14 (oom-hard). Mounts the w541 cache over sshfs at /mnt/auto/w541sstate (ro) and /mnt/auto/w541downloads (rw), bound into the container as /host-sstate and /host-downloads.
three_machine_architecture.e15: podman, same shape, but its mount paths DIFFER — check them on the machine. NOT oom-proof yet: the desktop still crashes above 12 threads under full load, so cap at 10. By moWerk's decision (2026-08-01) e15 is OMITTED from fat builds that would benefit from >10 threads until it is hardened.

podman_image_build_invocation.ownership_model: One agent session owns one build machine at a time, assigned by moWerk, because they share the w541's cache and tread on each other's devtool workspaces otherwise. Do not assume which machine is yours — ask. In 2026-08 two sessions each believed they owned the w541.
podman_image_build_invocation.clean_state_contract: Work in task-transient devtool workspaces and RESET THEM WHEN DONE, leaving a clean upstream build state for the next session. Check before starting: `devtool status` must say 'No recipes currently in your workspace'. Leftover workspaces silently contaminate the next session's build with unrelated patches — and if the leftover is in the component under investigation, it invalidates the experiment.
podman_image_build_invocation.devtool_reset_preserves: `devtool reset` does NOT delete the source tree: it moves it to build/workspace/attic/sources/<name>.<timestamp> and says so. Harmless, but the attic accumulates and is the caller's to clear.

stock_rom_dump_and_restore.scope: Dumping a watch's stock (WearOS) ROM and restoring it later. Distinct from device_flashing (flashing AsteroidOS onto a watch) and device_recovery (getting INTO fastboot). Derived 2026-08-02 from the OPPO factory package for beluga/belugaxl plus moWerk's own full-disk dumps; see porting_guide entry beluga_belugaxl_stock_rom_restore for the device specifics.
stock_rom_dump_and_restore.why_offer_this_at_all: moWerk's framing, and it is the right one: users ALREADY restore dumps unguided and fully brute-forced, then arrive in chat for help. The real baseline is not 'they abstain', it is 'they do it the worst possible way'. Withholding automation does not prevent the risky act. Do not reason against an imagined safe baseline.
stock_rom_dump_and_restore.authoritative_dump_sources: Dumps a-d-b made itself AND dumps made manually with hosttools. a-d-b's flashing code is based on hosttools and continues to be. Third-party dumps (e.g. XDA) are usable too — but see verify_the_artifact_not_the_provenance.

dump_methods._renamed: Was two_dump_methods until 2026-08-23, when a third method was recovered from the sol port. Three now.
dump_methods.ramdisk_clean: Boot a debug ramdisk so userdata is never mounted, then dump. Two dumps are byte-identical, so corruption is provable. NOT universally available: many manufacturers block `fastboot boot`, or the boot image refuses for superficial reasons. Availability is a PER-WATCH fact that must be established hands-on.
dump_methods.runtime_unclean: Put the watch in adb mode, place an AsteroidOS ext4 on userdata, reboot to bootloader, fastboot-boot the image so it comes up as a temporary install, then dump mmcblk0 from a root adb shell. Works broadly. The underlying disk is live, so a whole-disk checksum can never be reproduced.
dump_methods.initramfs_clean: THE ONE THAT WORKS WHEN ramdisk_clean CANNOT. Flash your OWN init_boot to the unused slot and boot THAT, rather than asking the bootloader to `fastboot boot` an unsigned image non-persistently. AsteroidOS's initramfs never mounts userdata, so the disk is quiescent and two dumps come out byte-identical, which is the whole value of ramdisk_clean, but it needs no bootloader cooperation beyond a normal flash. PROVEN on sol (Pixel Watch 3) 2026-08-08/09: two whole-disk dumps of 31406948352 bytes, 3834 s and 3839 s, IDENTICAL whole-image sha256 be53f3ed3000171e9a151f2e7615829cb1991d7c77583e94ee4d8f4bdfdca061, 81/81 partitions matching INCLUDING userdata; `mount` showed zero mmcblk0 entries for the whole capture. Transport was a single `adb exec-out dd` pipeline in a-d-b's own stockrom.dump_command form, and disk size was read from /sys/class/block/mmcblk0/size BEFORE the copy. This matters most on exactly the watches where ramdisk_clean is unavailable: sol's debug ramdisk arrives via the misc BCB and was never ours to trigger, so without this method sol could only ever have had a runtime_unclean dump.
dump_methods.artefact_and_manifest: sol's dump is on the w541 at /mnt/storage/sol-dumps/20260808/ (MANIFEST.txt, whole-image-sha256.txt, compare-report.txt, partitions.txt, per-device-state/ with 10 partitions, plus carved vendor_a.img and system_a.img). That MANIFEST follows this section's own dump_manifest_proposal and is the model to copy. Recovered 2026-08-23 by hunting for it: the method existed ONLY in that file, so neither the porting agent nor a-d-b could recall it. A dump whose method is not distilled here is a dump nobody can trust later, which is the manifest's own point: a filesystem timestamp is not a dump date, and the METHOD is what says which partitions may be trusted.
dump_methods.classify_lists_do_not_transfer: sol's MANIFEST flags this at a-d-b directly: classify()'s FIRMWARE / SAFE_ERASE / PER_DEVICE lists came from the OPPO beluga/belugaxl rawprogram manifest (MSM8909W), so on sol (monaco/SW5100, GKI, A/B slots, dynamic super) 69 of 81 names return `unknown`, and it does NOT know sol's sensorstore is per-device state. UNKNOWN MEANS UNCLASSIFIED, NOT SAFE. A UI built on this column must never present `unknown` as erasable.
dump_methods.record_availability_per_watch: 'Which dump methods does this watch support?' belongs in the fleet registry keyed by serial, and it is THREE questions now: can it `fastboot boot` a debug ramdisk (ramdisk_clean), can we flash our own init_boot to a spare slot (initramfs_clean), or is only runtime_unclean left. Originally recorded as the debug-ramdisk question alone — discovered once by hand, durable across reflashes, and then the UI knows rather than asks.

stock_rom_dump_and_restore.runtime_dumps_are_verifiable_PER_PARTITI: PROVEN 2026-08-03 on nemo <serial> (LG Watch Urbane 2nd Ed). Two independent runtime dumps over SSH, 12 minutes apart, 3909091328 bytes each, both complete. Whole-image sha256 DIFFER (as the wiki Backup Guide states). Per partition: 33 of 34 IDENTICAL bit-for-bit; the only one differing is userdata, the partition the running system writes to. So a runtime dump's whole-image checksum is worthless but every quiescent partition is verifiable, and taking TWO dumps tells you exactly which partitions you may trust - without an unlocked bootloader or the debug ramdisk. Corroboration: six 0.5 MiB partitions (fsc, ssd, DDR, keystore, keymasterb, cmnlibb) shared one hash because they are zero-filled - independently confirming the erase-class taxonomy taken from the vendor manifest.
stock_rom_dump_and_restore.verify_the_artifact_not_the_provenance: Provenance is unverifiable (anyone can rename a file); a dump is checkable. Use the same checks for a-d-b dumps, hosttools dumps and third-party images alike.

compatibility_check_two_gates.gate_1_gpt: Read the GPT out of the dump (LBA1 header, entries at LBA2) and off the live watch, and require an exact match on partition NAMES and LBAs. Cheap — needs only the first ~34 sectors — and a genuinely different device fails it immediately.
compatibility_check_two_gates.gate_1_is_NOT_sufficient: PROVEN 2026-08-02: beluga and belugaxl have byte-identical GPTs (same 40 partitions, same LBAs, same 14,942,208-sector disk). Two real variants can share one layout, so the GPT gate alone must never be the safety rule. An earlier claim that a wrong-model image 'fails this instantly' was wrong and was corrected by the data.
compatibility_check_two_gates.gate_2_fingerprint: The answer lives inside the system partition: ro.build.fingerprint, ro.product.device/name/model. Grep them straight out of the raw partition range (`grep -a` over the streamed region) — no mount needed. This is what actually establishes platform compatibility.

partition_classes._note: The manufacturer's own rawprogram XML makes this taxonomy obvious. Restore logic should be built on classes, not on a flat partition list.
partition_classes.firmware: system, vendor, boot, recovery, cache, oem, splash, LOGO, modem, and the bootloader chain (sbl1, aboot, rpm, tz, cmnlib, keymaster). Identical across units of one model — safe to take from a third-party image of the same platform.
partition_classes.per_device_state: persist, oppodycnvbk, oppostanvbk, modemst1/2, fsg, sec, devinfo. Sensor calibration, radio NV, device identity. NEVER share between watches, not even two identical units. Restoring a stranger's persist does not brick the watch — it silently replaces its calibration and identity, and nothing reports an error.
partition_classes.erase_do_not_restore: The factory flow ERASES these rather than writing them (no filename in rawprogram0.xml): opporeserve3, pad, modemst1, modemst2, misc, fsc, ssd, DDR, fsg, sec, devinfo, keystore, config (plus last_grow on LUN2). A naive 'restore every partition from my dump' does the opposite and writes stale state back underneath an otherwise-factory system.
partition_classes.user_data: userdata — see the empty_userdata rule, which is the single most important item here.

THE_EMPTY_USERDATA_RULE.rule: A stock restore must give userdata a FRESH EMPTY filesystem. Never restore a captured, populated userdata.
THE_EMPTY_USERDATA_RULE.evidence: The factory userdata.img is a 307 KB sparse image expanding to ~4.5 GB: 22 chunks of which ~13 blocks are metadata and the rest DONT_CARE — raw mkfs output containing no files. moWerk's own dump's userdata is a populated 4.3 GB f2fs from a provisioned watch. Both are valid f2fs; only the contents differ.
THE_EMPTY_USERDATA_RULE.symptom_when_violated: Boots far enough to show the WearOS spinning balls, then never completes setup — indefinitely. moWerk waited overnight on several attempts; a SUCCESSFUL restore takes about 20 minutes (xuv, 2026-06, after reverting a watch to WearOS with this method). If it has not finished in well under an hour it is stuck, not slow.
THE_EMPTY_USERDATA_RULE.mechanism: INFERRED, not proven from the bytes: userdata on this WearOS vintage is encrypted with keys bound to keystore/keymaster, and the factory flow ERASES keystore, config, devinfo and misc. A populated encrypted userdata under erased or mismatched key material cannot be decrypted, so setup loops forever.
THE_EMPTY_USERDATA_RULE.consequence: This explains why the community's 6-command fastboot recipe works and hand-rolled full restores fail: the recipe flashes the factory's EMPTY userdata.img and never touches the erase class.
THE_EMPTY_USERDATA_RULE.status: PROVEN 2026-08-03 on beluga 22979c8c. The full recipe — firmware from the owner's own dump plus the factory's EMPTY userdata, bootloader chain and per-device state untouched — restored a watch to stock on the first attempt, after moWerk had failed repeatedly over weeks by writing a captured userdata back. See porting_guide beluga_belugaxl_stock_rom_restore PROVEN_RECIPE, and asteroid-docking-bay stockrom.py.

stock_rom_dump_and_restore.dump_manifest_proposal: Write a small manifest beside every dump: codename, serial, partition table, per-partition checksums, dump method (ramdisk|runtime), per-partition verified flag, date, tool version. Then a runtime dump still reports WHICH partitions were provably clean instead of that distinction being lost when the file leaves the machine. Worth agreeing the format with hosttools early — retrofitting two tools later is far more expensive.
stock_rom_dump_and_restore.a_dump_carries_its_own_partition_map: Dissection needs no external table: everything required is in the dump's own GPT in the first 34 sectors. This is what MagneFire's dissect script (used by beroset's hosttools) works from.
stock_rom_dump_and_restore.silent_failure_seen_in_the_wild: ~/Git/asteroid-hosttools/original-sprat.img is 0 bytes — a backup that looks present in `ls` and contains nothing. A recorded size and checksum makes that instantly detectable; a directory listing never will.
stock_rom_dump_and_restore.backup_before_flashing: The highest-value feature built on all of this: it makes flashing reversible, which lowers the stakes of every other operation offered to a novice.
stock_rom_dump_and_restore.attribution: Mechanism derived by Claude under moWerk's direction, 2026-08-02, from files on disk (OPPO factory package + moWerk's beluga/belugaxl dumps). Community 6-command fastboot recipe: MagneWater on reddit (very likely MagneFire). 20-minute restore duration: xuv. Dissect script: MagneFire, used in beroset's hosttools.
stock_rom_dump_and_restore.back_up_per_device_state_first: Before any write, pull the target's OWN per-device partitions (persist, oppodycnvbk, oppostanvbk, modemst1/2, fsg, sec, devinfo) with `adb exec-out dd`. ~60 MB, seconds, and it is the only data in the whole operation that no other dump can replace.
stock_rom_dump_and_restore.minimal_restore_of_a_permanent_asteroido: SCOPE: older watches only - NOT beluga-class, see DO_NOT_REDUCE_A_RECIPE_THAT_WORKS. A permanent AsteroidOS install writes exactly TWO partitions: `fastboot flash userdata <rootfs.ext4>` and `fastboot flash boot <boot.img>`. So undoing it should need only a stock boot plus a wiped userdata - and rather than sourcing an empty userdata image, flash stock boot then `adb reboot recovery` and factory-reset, letting the DEVICE format userdata with whatever filesystem it expects (recovery is untouched by an AsteroidOS install, so it is always available). moWerk's deduction 2026-08-03, supported by dump analysis - nemo's system/recovery/modem are all still stock while boot carries the AsteroidOS cmdline (selinux=0 SYSTEMD_CGROUP_ENABLE). INFERRED AND UNTESTED end to end. Do not apply it to a watch whose restore has a working recipe already.

DO_NOT_REDUCE_A_RECIPE_THAT_WORKS.rule: moWerk, 2026-08-03: the beluga restore sequence is CANON. Do not shorten it because some partitions look unmodified. He had tried many ways to reflash a beluga and failed every time; the sequence that finally worked may be a chain of DEVICE-SPECIFIC NECESSITIES whose reasons are not yet understood.
DO_NOT_REDUCE_A_RECIPE_THAT_WORKS.canon_sequence: beluga: flash boot, system, vendor, recovery, cache from a stock full-disk dump, then the factory EMPTY userdata.img. Bootloader chain and per-device state untouched. Proven on 22979c8c 2026-08-03, first attempt.
DO_NOT_REDUCE_A_RECIPE_THAT_WORKS.why_this_rule_exists: 'That partition was never modified, so it need not be restored' is a deduction, not an observation. It is probably right for older watches and it is NOT established for beluga-class devices. A restore recipe is validated end to end or not at all; trimming it turns a proven procedure back into a hypothesis.
what_might_actually_be_going_on_UNPROVEN: SELinux context: unclean writes may leave files outside their expected context, and a newer WearOS may then refuse them. Completely unproven - moWerk's hypothesis.
Key provisioning tied to the encrypted userdata, such that partitions beyond boot must be written for the device to re-provision cleanly. No evidence either way.

two_classes_of_watch.older_watches: moWerk's long-standing assumption that `system` must be flashed back appears to be FALSE for these. The minimal method (stock boot + wiped userdata) is likely sufficient - but still untested end to end.
two_classes_of_watch.newer_soc_wearos: beluga-class. Use the canon sequence. Something further is going on here that is not yet identified.

stock_rom_dump_and_restore.RESTORE_RECIPES_DO_NOT_TRANSFER_BETWEEN_: moWerk, 2026-08-03: 'please stop with bogus transfer of knowledge from the beluga case to any other watch. beluga is a total outlier in the fleet.' Each device gets its OWN recorded canon, derived from a sequence that actually worked on THAT device - never by reasoning from another one's. Claude applied beluga's partition set to nemo twice in one day and was wrong both times. See porting_guide beluga_belugaxl_stock_rom_restore and nemo_stock_rom_restore; note they differ in step order, in wipe method and in which partitions are written.

platform_and_build.build_dies_with_SIGTERM_check_earlyoom_F: DIAGNOSTIC, findable from the AsteroidOS side because that is where a build session looks. A Yocto task that dies with 'fatal error: Terminated signal terminated program cc1plus' plus "{standard input}: Error: open CFI at the end of file; missing .cfi_endproc directive" is almost certainly EARLYOOM, not a compiler, toolchain or icecc fault. The tells: SIGTERM not SIGKILL (the kernel OOM killer uses SIGKILL), and a truncated assembler stream because cc1plus died mid-output while piping to as. THE TRAP: earlyoom logs ONLY to its own systemd unit and leaves NO kernel OOM entries whatsoever, so `journalctl -k | grep -i oom` returns nothing and the cause looks like a ghost. CHECK: journalctl -u earlyoom --since '3 hours ago'. earlyoom's --prefer list starts with ^(cc1|cc1plus|ld|make|bitbake|...) so a compiler is the FIRST thing it reaches for. That is correct behaviour and protects the desktop and the filesystem; losing a build is far better than the July 2026 outcome where the kernel OOM killer fired mid-btrfs-transaction and corrupted the filesystem. Just retry the build, and check that --cgroup-parent=build.slice was passed. Confirmed 2026-08-08 on the p14s: killed a clang-native LLVM compile mid-build. Full detail: mo-infrastructure/build_environment.json -> icecc_distributed_compiling -> earlyoom_kills_look_like_icecc_faults.

usb3_hub_shared_vbus_companion.summary: On a USB3-connected hub VBUS is shared between a USB2 port and its USB3 companion; cutting only one side leaves VBUS up.
usb3_hub_shared_vbus_companion.sysfs_disable_reaches: Only the sides linked by the kernel port 'peer' symlink. Root-connected hubs expose the peer at every level (both disable attrs reachable).
usb3_hub_shared_vbus_companion.behind_a_dock_gotcha: A hub cascaded behind a dock (rig Hub B: 1-9.1.3.x behind the Lenovo 17ef dock) exposes NO leaf 'peer' and NO USB3-side sysfs interface (3-5.1.3.3:1.0 absent). sysfs can cut only the USB2 side; the set falsely confirms while VBUS stays up. Symptoms: shelve only reboots the watch; live ports read off while physically powered (USB2 link down => not enumerated => reads disconnected).
usb3_hub_shared_vbus_companion.fix: uhubctl is companion-aware: one 'uhubctl -l <hub> -p <n> -a off' cuts BOTH sides on both direct and behind-dock hubs, AND updates the sysfs disable so the fast read stays correct. In a-d-b, gate the sysfs fast path on _sysfs_power_is_complete() (>=2 disable paths, or no USB3 companion) and fall through to uhubctl otherwise.
usb3_hub_shared_vbus_companion.verified: 2026-07-24 on the rig through a-d-b uhubctl_set_power: Hub B port OFF => USB2 disable=1 AND USB3 '00a0 off'; ON brings both up.

plug_a16_hubs_into_usb2_host_ports.rule: Plug the A16 (Realtek RTS5411 0bda:5411) smart hubs into USB 2.0 host ports, NOT USB 3.0 SuperSpeed ports.
plug_a16_hubs_into_usb2_host_ports.why: A USB3 host port makes the hub present a SuperSpeed companion (a 3-x bus twin) that SHARES the physical VBUS with the USB2 side. That companion is the root of every power problem: (1) cutting only the USB2-side sysfs disable leaves VBUS up on the companion (the shelve-doesn't-cut crisis); (2) behind a dock the companion has no sysfs at all, forcing slow uhubctl; (3) on replug the kernel can tear the USB2<->USB3 port 'peer' links and DROP the deep-leaf port-disable attrs entirely, so those ports cannot switch at all until a reboot/replug.
plug_a16_hubs_into_usb2_host_ports.usb2_is_clean: On a USB2 host port there is no companion: every hub port exposes a writable `disable` (via the udev rule), switching is instant sysfs, no uhubctl, no peer fragility. Watches are USB2 devices — USB3 buys nothing here.
plug_a16_hubs_into_usb2_host_ports.detect: A16 on USB3 => a sibling 3-x hub exists (e.g. 1-2 has companion 3-2) and deep-leaf ports may lack `disable`. A16 on USB2 => no 3-x twin, every leaf `disable` present + writable.
plug_a16_hubs_into_usb2_host_ports.confirmed: Rig, 2026-07-25: A16 #2 moved from a dock USB3 port to a laptop USB2 port (1-3) => no 3-3 companion, all disable attrs writable, instant sysfs on/off verified. A16 #1 left on USB3 (1-2, companion 3-2): after the replug its 1-2.3.3 deep-leaf `disable` attrs were GONE, uhubctl blocked over ssh by uaccess => those ports unswitchable.
plug_a16_hubs_into_usb2_host_ports.uaccess_note: The udev rule uses TAG+=uaccess, which grants USB device access only to the ACTIVE LOCAL session — uhubctl SET run over ssh fails 'permission problems'. sysfs `disable` (chmod g+w, group users) is the path that works headless; keep sysfs switchable (USB2 ports) rather than relying on uhubctl.

dont_poll_empty_ports_discover_device_si.rule: Do NOT poll empty hub ports (reading their `disable` power attr). Discover watches from the DEVICE side — a watch appearing on ADB/SSH → resolve its sysfs port — and poll only OCCUPIED ports.
dont_poll_empty_ports_discover_device_si.why: Reading an empty port's `disable` attr is slow (hangs for seconds on a powered-down port) AND, on flaky A16/USB3-companion hubs, renegotiates the whole tree — which knocks the OTHER watches off the bus ('power/read an empty port → the hub drops everyone'). A background warmer doing this per empty port is both a latency source and actively destructive.
dont_poll_empty_ports_discover_device_si.occupied_ports_are_cheap: A present child device at `<hub>.<port>` already proves the port is powered — no `disable` read needed. So the status path can stay fast without touching empty ports at all.
dont_poll_empty_ports_discover_device_si.onboarding_pattern: Fill a rig with the interactive 'onboard sweep': map topology → power ALL sockets down → equip every socket (a dark port doesn't enumerate → no ADB flood) → run ONE port at a time: power on → detect ADB (else SSH/RNDIS 192.168.2.15 → allocate unique IP → adb-or-keep-ssh per prefer-ADB) → map + first data + registry.note → PPPS test → clean poweroff → cut VBUS → next. Never >1 port powered.
dont_poll_empty_ports_discover_device_si.burst_crashes_adb: Powering many ports on at once = ~24 watches enumerate in a burst that crashes the adb server (kill/start-server to recover). Always serialize; never bulk-power-on.

xhci_device_slot_exhaustion.rule: An Intel xHCI host controller has a hard device-slot limit (32 on 8-Series/Lynx Point, w541). EVERY enumerated device holds a slot - including every internal hub chip of a cascaded 'smart hub' and, on a USB3 host port, its SuperSpeed companion twin. When the bus is full the next device gets 'Not enough host controller resources for new device state' / "can't set config #1, error -12": it enumerates (address, descriptors, answers lsusb -v) but NO configuration is applied, so NO interfaces exist - invisible to adb, fastboot, and any interface-descriptor-based detection, while the kernel retries every ~67s (bus churn).
xhci_device_slot_exhaustion.arithmetic: One RSHTECH A16 16-port = FIVE cascaded Realtek RTS5411 4-port chips (root + 2 mid + 2 deep). On a USB3 host port each chip enumerates twice (USB2 + SS companion) = 10 slots per box with zero watches. Two A16s on USB3 + Lenovo dock + laptop peripherals = ~25 slots overhead, leaving ~7 for watches on a 32-slot controller.
xhci_device_slot_exhaustion.symptoms_it_masquerades_as: flaky 8th watch / 'brownout' with a healthy PSU; watches that 'never enumerate' during onboarding while actually live on the bus; adb server 'wedge' that a server restart doesn't fix; onboarding timeouts; reconnects that idle out.
xhci_device_slot_exhaustion.diagnose: journalctl -k | grep 'can.t set config' ; count slots: ls /sys/bus/usb/devices | grep -E '^[13]-[0-9.]+$' | wc -l (adjust bus numbers to the xHCI's buses); a starved device has no :1.0 interface dirs but answers lsusb -v.
xhci_device_slot_exhaustion.mitigations: free slots: plug hub uplinks into USB2-only host ports (halves hub slots - see plug_a16_hubs_into_usb2_host_ports, now doubly justified) or unbind idle SS companion trees; keep watches truly shelved so concurrent enumerated count stays low; ultimate: route hub ports to the EHCI controller via Intel XUSB2PR setpci (EHCI has no slot concept). VBUS-switching behaviour with the SS side unbound is UNVERIFIED - test before relying.
xhci_device_slot_exhaustion.confirmed: w541 rig, 2026-07-25 audit (docs/audits/2026-07-25-usb-brittleness-xhci-slots.md, asteroid-docking-bay): exactly 32 devices on buses 1+3, three watches live-but-unconfigured in an hours-long retry storm.

ghost_nodes_after_a_move_adb_is_the_arbi.rule: When a watch is moved between ports, its OLD sysfs node can survive if the hub never raises a disconnect — the same serial then appears at two paths at once. Use `adb devices -l` as the arbiter: where it names a path for a serial, that path is live BY CONSTRUCTION, and any other path claiming that serial is a leftover.
ghost_nodes_after_a_move_adb_is_the_arbi.why_it_is_hard: The two nodes are indistinguishable by inspection — sparrow's ghost and its real node both reported cfg=1, auth=1, speed=480 (2026-07-31). No property of the node itself gives it away, so an 'unconfigured device' check cannot catch it.
ghost_nodes_after_a_move_adb_is_the_arbi.symptom: The UI appears to swap two watches' identities on every refresh. It is not flapping: the backend is stable and ONE watch simply occupies TWO rows, which reads as swapping at a glance.
ghost_nodes_after_a_move_adb_is_the_arbi.fallback: When adb has no opinion (fastboot, or a dead adb server), keep BOTH nodes — guessing is worse than showing two. And name the ghost rather than hiding it: a port that lies about being empty is the opposite bug.

count_reenumerations_to_find_a_bad_cradl.rule: Count `add` events per hub port (udev, or `new high-speed USB device` in dmesg). A watch that docks once and stays put enumerates ONCE; every enumeration after that is the connection failing and recovering. Subtract that first one so a healthy port reads 0, and reset the tally on any power change so your own shelve/cycle does not inflate it.
count_reenumerations_to_find_a_bad_cradl.why: A failing cradle otherwise only ever produces an impression ('that one is flakey'). The kernel has been counting the whole time and nobody reads it. On the w541 rig this turned three separate cradle faults from hunches into a diagnosis in one pass.
count_reenumerations_to_find_a_bad_cradl.signature_of_a_data_fault: `device descriptor read/64, error -71` and `device not accepting address` mean the DATA lines are bad while VBUS is fine — exactly what a broken cradle lead or a bent connector produces. A watch charging happily with no adb is this.
count_reenumerations_to_find_a_bad_cradl.the_invisible_case: A cradle bad enough that enumeration NEVER completes produces no repeat successes at all — the host sees nothing while the watch shows adb popups on its own screen. Such a watch cannot be the enumeration spammer; only the watch knows it is being plugged in.
count_reenumerations_to_find_a_bad_cradl.verified: 2026-07-31 — the rig's worst offender was a wren at 43 of the last 80 enumerations, found by hand-counting dmesg before this was automated

hub_vbus_capability_by_chip.summary: uhubctl marking a hub 'ppps' does NOT mean it cuts VBUS. Several chips report per-port power switching, transition state cleanly and exit 0, yet leave the 5V pin live so a connected watch keeps charging while only the DATA lines drop. The distinction is per silicon, established 2026-07-02 (raw log: investigation-logs/usb-hubs/hardware_findings.md; uhubctl issues #664/#665, both filed by moWerk and closed after real VBUS testing).
hub_vbus_capability_by_chip.how_a_ppps_false_positive_happens: Testing on an EMPTY port looks correct because there is no device whose charging you can observe. A real VBUS test needs a device connected and its charge indicator watched (a cable with a power LED is ideal). #664/#665 were both filed on empty-port evidence and retracted once a watch was actually charging through an 'off' port.

true_vbus_switching.17ef:1014 / 17ef:1015: Lenovo ThinkPad USB 3.0 Ultra Dock DK-1523 (root / sub-hub). CONFIRMED true per-port VBUS: narwhal's cable power-LED went dark instantly on `uhubctl -l 1-2 -p 2 -a off`. First fleet hub to do real VBUS switching. Watches enumerate on the USB2 companion bus (1-2 / 1-2.4).
true_vbus_switching.RSHTECH A-16: On the uhubctl compatible list as full per-port PPPS; the fleet's main VBUS-switching hub since. (See the separate xhci_device_slot_exhaustion entry for its host-side cost.)
true_vbus_switching.known_good_reference: Yepkit YKUSH (explicit per-port VBUS), Acroname USB 3.1 (gold standard). Ref: github.com/mvp/uhubctl#compatible-usb-hubs.

data_line_disconnect_only.05e3:0606: ALCOR 'USB Hub 2.0', generic 4-port (x4 units on the old rig). Marked ppps, but VBUS stays live on 'off' — data lines drop (adb/enumeration go), watch keeps charging. lsusb misIDs it as D-Link DUB-H4 (the real DUB-H4 is 05e3:0608). Useful for adb ops (reboot/bootloader/flash), useless for charge management. uhubctl issue #664.
data_line_disconnect_only.2109:2813: VIA Labs root of the Manhattan MondoHub II 28-port. Group-switching port 2 of this root powers the whole 28-port cascade on/off, but it is data-line-only — VBUS stays live. Same chip ships in Aukey CB-C59 / AmazonBasics U3-7HUB. uhubctl issue #665.
data_line_disconnect_only.214b:7250: Huasheng sub-hubs cascaded under the MondoHub II VIA root (x6). GANGED — no per-port software switching at all; the front-panel rocker switches are mechanical only and cannot be driven via uhubctl.

hub_vbus_capability_by_chip.rule_of_thumb: Before trusting a hub for charge/shelve management, VBUS-test it with a watch connected and its charge LED watched. 'ppps' + clean transitions + exit 0 prove the data-line switch, not the power switch. LEDs are truth; the register can be lying.

a_physical_box_is_several_hub_entries.summary: One physical hub box registers as SEVERAL cascaded hub entries, and auto-naming gives them all the same name. Measured on the w541 rig 2026-08-09: the Sabrent is five entries (1-6 root with 0 ports, plus 1-6.1..1-6.4 with 4 ports each); the A16 #2 is five (1-3, 1-3.3, 1-3.3.3, 1-3.3.4, 1-3.4); the Lenovo dock is two (1-9, 1-9.4).
a_physical_box_is_several_hub_entries.why_it_bites: Anything that addresses 'a hub' by one location acts on one CHIP, not the box the operator sees. Hiding the Sabrent took five clicks, and the first looked like a no-op because the box ROOT carries no ports — only its own header row went away. Each later click removed exactly one 4-port chip, so rows vanished four at a time.
a_physical_box_is_several_hub_entries.and_the_names_collide: Because every chip in a box shares the auto-assigned name, any UI keyed on the display name collapses them. In a-d-b's row reconciler that silently dropped four of five headers. Key on the ADDRESS; a box name is not unique by construction.
a_physical_box_is_several_hub_entries.rule: Address a box by its root and everything cascaded under it — root = location.split('.')[0], then match root itself plus anything starting root+'.'. Set the whole box to one state rather than toggling per chip, or a box whose chips disagree stays mixed forever.

vbus_and_data_are_separate_and_the_watch.summary: A USB port carries power and data independently. A hub's per-port switch cuts VBUS; the D+/D- pair runs through the hub silicon and is not switched. A watch with a charged battery can therefore keep its gadget up with zero volts on the power pin and stay fully adb-reachable. Measured on the w541 A16 2026-08-16: sol reported /sys/class/power_supply/*/online = 0 on every supply while adb talked to it normally, with the port's physical button off and its LED dark.
vbus_and_data_are_separate_and_the_watch.why_it_bites: The LED tells you POWER, never PRESENCE. A row that persists on a port whose LED is dark looks exactly like a stale kernel node, and cost an hour of chasing a phantom. It is also the reverse hazard: a watch left on a buttoned-off port is awake and draining, not shelved.
vbus_and_data_are_separate_and_the_watch.how_to_tell: Ask the watch: /sys/class/power_supply/*/online is 1 while external power is present and 0 without it, independent of charge level (a Full battery still reads 1). No host-side register can answer this - on the A16 the hub reports the port as powered while the physical button has cut it.
vbus_and_data_are_separate_and_the_watch.important_scope: This is NOT how a-d-b's software power-off behaves. Writing the port's `disable` attribute, or uhubctl's power-off, takes the PORT down - data path included - so the device disconnects. That is why two months of shelving watches produced no stray adb traffic. Only the hardware button (a switch in the VBUS rail, downstream of the hub silicon) separates the two.
vbus_and_data_are_separate_and_the_watch.consequence_for_drain_tests: There is no standard USB request for 'cut power, keep data', so a drain test cannot poll battery over USB without also charging. The route that does work is Orbit: unplug and poll over WiFi/SSH.
vbus_and_data_are_separate_and_the_watch.confidence: observation confirmed on hardware; the mechanism (hardware VBUS switch downstream of the hub) is inferred from that observation plus USB behaviour. The device-specific half is suspect - see sol_port_findings.

adb_shell_expands_globs_on_the_HOST.summary: a-d-b's adb_shell builds `adb -s SER shell <cmd>` and runs it through a host shell. An unescaped `*` therefore expands against the HOST's filesystem before the watch ever sees it. Measured 2026-08-16: `cat /sys/class/power_supply/*/online` shipped the laptop's own supply names (AC, BAT0) to the watch, which answered 'No such file'.
adb_shell_expands_globs_on_the_HOST.why_it_bites: Silent and misleading - the failure is indistinguishable from a watch that has no such nodes. Escape the glob (`\*`) so the watch's shell expands it, or wrap the whole command in double quotes, which also suppresses host expansion (battery_and_screen does this and is correct as it stands).

dumpsys_is_android_only.summary: AsteroidOS is plain Linux: no getprop, no dumpsys. a-d-b's adb_external_power asked `dumpsys battery` and so returned None on every AsteroidOS watch since it was written - it is the corroborating half of the PPPS verdict, and it verified nothing while appearing cautious. Fixed 2026-08-16 to read the kernel power_supply class first, keeping dumpsys for Wear OS reference units.
dumpsys_is_android_only.related: Wear OS watches DO answer `getprop ro.product.device`, and it returns the same codename AsteroidOS uses, because the port takes the vendor's.
dumpsys_is_android_only.confidence: confirmed - `dumpsys: command not found` on sturgeon

a_ppps_announcement_is_a_claim_not_a_ver.summary: The `ppps` flag comes from uhubctl reading the hub descriptor: the hub ANNOUNCES per-port power switching. A hub can acknowledge a power command and flip its status bit with VBUS still hot, so the announcement is not proof. The verdict needs a watch on the port and the watch's own answer about external power.
a_ppps_announcement_is_a_claim_not_a_ver.layers: a-d-b's test_port_power_switching has three: descriptor capability, a register gate that returns dumb unless both off and on confirm, and the watch-side corroboration (which was dead fleet-wide until 2026-08-16, see dumpsys_is_android_only).
a_ppps_announcement_is_a_claim_not_a_ver.rig_note: On the w541 the A16 (Realtek RTS5411) announces and switches; the Sabrent (Genesys) does not announce and is treated as dumb; the Lenovo dock does not announce yet moWerk reports 4 switchable ports - announcement and reality diverge in BOTH directions.
a_ppps_announcement_is_a_claim_not_a_ver.confidence: confirmed by reading the code and the rig's descriptors

ncm_watches_offer_adb_and_ssh_together.summary: Configfs-era watches (aurora 5.15.x, sol 5.15.148) run ffs.adb and ncm.0 in ONE composite gadget, so ADB and the network link are live simultaneously. The either/or model every USB-mode path in a-d-b was built on does not apply to them. Proven on the rig 2026-08-16 by the porting session: an ssh console open while a-d-b showed the watch adb-connected.
ncm_watches_offer_adb_and_ssh_together.switching_is_destructive: usb-moded's developer_mode.ini asks for `rndis`, and these kernels have no rndis configfs function (CONFIG_USB_CONFIGFS_RNDIS unset). usb-moded falls back to the charging-only 0afe composition: no adb, no net, no remote recovery, reboot required. a-d-b's switch ops and its stray peeler now refuse when a watch offers both.

detect_by_interface_class_never_idProduc.02/0d/00: CDC-NCM control - the ssh-capable network function
detect_by_interface_class_never_idProduc.0a/00/01: CDC data belonging to the above
detect_by_interface_class_never_idProduc.08: mass storage only - the dead fallback composition
detect_by_interface_class_never_idProduc.rule: 0afe is AMBIGUOUS: 0afe + ff/42/01 is a healthy initramfs-style composition; 0afe with ONLY mass storage is the dead fallback. A port power cycle cannot fix the dead one - the problem is the gadget composition, not the enumeration - so recommend a REBOOT rather than offering a cycle that silently does nothing. Never infer boot state from idProduct: it is a userspace artefact and can be stale while the system is healthy.

reach_it_over_IPv6_LINK_LOCAL_no_address.summary: sshd.socket listens on [::]:22 and both ends have link-local with disable_ipv6=0. Measured end to end 2026-08-16: `ping -6 ff02::1%<iface>` answers, `ip -6 neigh` gives the peer, and TCP to [fe80::...%iface]:22 returns a real SSH-2.0-OpenSSH_9.9 banner - with NO address configured anywhere and NO root.
reach_it_over_IPv6_LINK_LOCAL_no_address.why_it_matters_for_a-d-b: a-d-b runs UNPRIVILEGED (rootless port switching via udev rules). The originally proposed per-watch /30 scheme needed host-side `ip addr add`, i.e. a privileged helper, polkit rule or networkd file. Link-local removes that requirement entirely, and the scope-id (%iface) makes collisions structurally impossible - which also retires the multiple-interfaces-on-one-/24 ARP hazard.
reach_it_over_IPv6_LINK_LOCAL_no_address.connect_form: ssh -6 ceres@fe80::...%iface   (NOTE the user is ceres, not root - every SSH path in a-d-b currently hardcodes root@)
reach_it_over_IPv6_LINK_LOCAL_no_address.the_address_is_NOT_stable: The link-local is EUI-64 derived from the usb0 MAC, and the kernel generates that MAC randomly every time the ncm function is created - i.e. every boot. Do not cache the address; rediscover per boot with one multicast ping. Cache the hub:port -> iface mapping, which is stable. The porting session can pin dev_addr from the device DSN to make it deterministic per watch (asked for: it would give a-d-b a stable identity that is NOT the USB serial).
reach_it_over_IPv6_LINK_LOCAL_no_address.supersedes: The static IPv4 defaults (aurora 192.168.42.2, sol 192.168.43.2) and the /30-pool plan in the porting notes' 8.4/8.5 - harmless as a fallback, needed by nothing.

ncm_watches_offer_adb_and_ssh_together.not_every_watch: Legacy android_usb 4.9 watches (beluga, rubyfish/rover) have no configfs gadget and no NCM at all. Gate any ssh-over-USB affordance on being configfs-era, not on 'newer port'.
ncm_watches_offer_adb_and_ssh_together.state_is_passively_observable: NCM ACTIVE is readable from the descriptors (02/0d present, cdc_ncm bound) at zero cost and always fresh. Only 'capable but not active' needs the on-device probe (mkdir /config/usb_gadget/g1/functions/ncm.test then rmdir, non-destructive). Key any cache on hub:port plus something that changes on reflash (VERSION_ID / uname -r) - NOT on the USB serial, which aurora proved can be a kernel cmdline fragment for an entire session.
ncm_watches_offer_adb_and_ssh_together.current_rig_state_2026_08_16: aurora and sol have NCM enabled at RUNTIME via systemd-run, which does not survive a reboot. Until an image shipping the *-usb-network units is flashed, a-d-b will see 'capable but not active' after every boot on both. The units auto-enable in the built images, so a-d-b's job is detect-and-connect only - never enable the function or touch configfs.
ncm_watches_offer_adb_and_ssh_together.confidence: measured end to end by the porting session and cross-checked against a-d-b's constraints

charging_can_latch_at_idle_current.summary: A docked watch can report status=Charging with a healthy VBUS while drawing only idle current and delivering NOTHING to its pack. Measured on aurora 2026-08-19: port offered 500 mA, watch drew 60 mA, battery/current_now was 0, and it lost ~1% every few hours over 2.6 days.
charging_can_latch_at_idle_current.the_tell: The PAIR of readings, not either alone: usb/current_now at tens of mA AND battery/current_now == 0. `status` lies here -- it said Charging throughout, and the second gauge (sw5100_bms) said 'Not charging' at the same moment.
charging_can_latch_at_idle_current.what_it_rules_out: Not supply: the port held 4.92 V while the watch drew a ninth of its allowance, and another watch on the same A16 box was simultaneously at 100%. A hub that cannot keep up shows the opposite -- device pulls its full limit, voltage sags.
charging_can_latch_at_idle_current.recovery: One port power cycle. VBUS off/on re-runs charger detection: 60 -> 199 mA on USB and 0 -> 60 mA into the pack, immediately, with no reboot and no reconnection. The lighter intervention is sufficient; a reboot was never needed.
charging_can_latch_at_idle_current.consequences: Charge targets never complete and drain tests are meaningless on a watch in this state, and it is invisible unless battery/current_now is read.
charging_can_latch_at_idle_current.owner: watch side (charger detection / HAL) - moWerk's read. a-d-b's part is detecting and surfacing it.
charging_can_latch_at_idle_current.confidence: confirmed on hardware, with a same-hub control
